🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.34% (intraday, 7-year +19bp). At trading day 13 (last close) it was -1.62% against a five-campaign average of -0.37% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.35%. The 10-year is +25bp since the hike vs a +6bp campaign average at the same point.
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 696bp against a five-year average of 408bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +42bp and BB +34bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.28 → 0.49 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+2bp).
  • Stocks: Stock futures point higher after US indexes gained yesterday and Europe trades up.
  • FX: The dollar is weaker this morning; the euro and pound are both up.
  • Technicals: US stocks are far above their usual trend, so a pullback is more likely.
  • Sectors: Tech has led for a month while banks, real estate and utilities lag.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most corporate borrowing is still cheap, but the riskiest junk borrowers are paying much more.
  • Crisis: Systemic stress looks moderate: the war, deficits and the weakest junk bonds are the risks.
  • Inflation: Underlying inflation is easing slowly but still runs above the Fed's 2% target.
  • Tech Bubble: Stock prices aren't at 2000 extremes, but credit and volatility are just as complacent.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Delta reports Thursday and JPMorgan next Tuesday; the big IPOs this week are mostly outside the US.
  • Iran: Hormuz stays shut while Iran weighs a US reply, and tankers keep getting hit.
  • Warsh: Warsh is still fighting inflation; another rate hike is possible, but this is our estimate.
  • Outlook: Short term: modestly positive. Over the coming months: guarded, because credit stress is spreading.
  • Trades: Cut the riskiest junk bonds, buy Treasuries, and wait for a dip before buying stocks.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 24 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Pre-market: Both watchlists are empty and that is the right answer today. Nice tape, nothing to trade from this scan, keep your hands in your pockets.
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.84 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 99th pctile, +3bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Enjoy the rally, but watch junk-bond stress spreading toward better-quality bonds.

The biggest story this morning is the energy unwind. Brent is down 3.07% to 97.24 and WTI is down 2.71% to 87.01. That pulls Treasury yields lower: the 10Y is 5.2688 (-3.58bp), the 2Y 4.7871 (-2.51bp) and the 30Y 5.6414. The softer dollar (DXY 101.839, -0.32%) and the bid in gold (4170.37, +0.75%) fit the same rates-relief story. Futures are extending yesterday's gains: in the prior session the S&P 500 rose +0.66% to 7773.95, the Nasdaq +1.05% to 27477.31 and the Russell 2000 +0.50%. This morning ES is +0.43% (7859.75), NQ +0.55% and Dow futures +0.51%. Europe is firm, with the Euro Stoxx 50 +0.38% and the STOXX 600 +0.41%. Sentiment is calm, with the VIX at 15.31. The oil drop is notable because the Iran war has not de-escalated: the Strait of Hormuz remains shut pending Iranian conditions, and tankers were struck near Hormuz over the weekend. The one thing that should temper the risk-on mood is credit's weakest corner. In the computed HY contagion panel, the Caa–B spread gap is 696bp, against a 5-year average of about 408bp. That puts it in about the 99.8th percentile of the last five years and makes it the widest since April 2020. It has widened 174bp in three months. The question is whether this is spreading. Single-B has widened 42bp in a month (to 296bp) and Ba 34bp (to 185bp). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily moves has risen to 0.49, from 0.28 three months ago, but it is still below its 0.70 five-year median. So stress is starting to move up the quality ladder in price, but the move is not yet broad: B and Ba are still below their 5-year averages, and IG (82bp, +2bp in a month) is barely affected. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Over one month the US leadership is clearly growth-led: Info Tech +6.5% and Comm Services +2.9%. Rate-sensitive and credit-sensitive groups are being sold: Financials -7.78%, Real Estate -7.69%, Utilities -6.66%, Materials -4.98%, Cons Discr -4.29%, Cons Staples -3.42% and Health Care -3.22%. Defensives (Staples, Health Care, Utilities) are not acting as havens, which points to a rates story rather than a growth scare. Weak Financials alongside a positively sloped curve suggests markets are pricing credit-quality worries more than margin tailwinds. Year to date, Energy (+38.72%) and Info Tech (+31.07%) dominate, while Utilities (-7.51%) and Cons Discr (-3.73%) trail. The global picture is the same: Info Tech +6.67% in a month and +38.86% YTD, with Financials -6.72% and Real Estate -7.05% over the month. Yesterday's broad gains (Materials +1.22%, Comm Services +1.14%, Energy +0.89%) were risk-on, with only Real Estate down (-0.44%). Net: growth over value, cyclicals mixed, and defensives offering no shelter while yields stay high.

The Caa OAS is 992bp (+123bp in a month, +202bp in three months; 94th percentile over 5 years) and the Caa–B gap is 696bp (99.8th 5-year percentile, widest since April 2020). FRED's ICE CCC–B gap is 890bp, at its 100th percentile, and CCC sits at 1202bp. Contagion is visible in price: B is +42bp in a month to 296bp, Ba +34bp to 185bp, and the HY–IG gap +38bp to 225bp. Levels are still below the 5-year averages (B 348bp, Ba 219bp), and the B–Ba gap of 111bp is below its 129bp average. The Caa/B correlation of daily moves has risen to 0.49 (from 0.28 three months ago) but remains under its 0.70 median. Levels to watch: US HY OAS moving above about 3.5% (the B average of about 348bp would need to be reached), and IG moving above about 1.0% (its 5-year average is near 102bp). Either would most likely come from oil re-spiking on Hormuz or a default event in the CCC cohort spilling into single-B refinancing. A move in IG toward its 0.71% historical tight looks unlikely while CCC deteriorates.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.84 vol points (49th percentile of the 35 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 113.6 (83th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 118bp (steeper by 43bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (89bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — Moderately sticky but cooling. Every computed underlying-inflation measure is trending lower, and the median/trimmed-mean gauges sit around 2.2–2.7%, near the middle of their own history. Headline-relevant core PCE (3.01%) is still well above target, and the Dallas Fed distribution shows a fat fast-rising tail: 13.2% of the basket is inflating above 10% and 15.7% at 5–10%. The trend is improving, but breadth and energy keep the Fed wary.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Today's market resembles the 1997–98 phase of the dot-com run more than March 2000. The current Nasdaq path, indexed to Oct-2022, has reached about 250 after 48 months. On the 1990-anchored panel the dot-com path peaked at month 113 (1423.9), and on the 1994-anchored panel at month 69. Leadership is concentrated: we estimate about 40% of the S&P 500 in the top 10 names, and a CAPE near 40 (estimate). The CAPE is roughly 25-year highs, though still short of the 2000 extreme. The Buffett indicator is above 200% (estimate), while ex-mega-caps it is closer to 140–160% according to cited analysis. What is missing versus 2000 is retail euphoria (AAII bull–bear -11.9) and IPO mania (this week's pipeline is modest and mostly offshore). Margin debt growth of 33.7% YoY is 46% of the way to the 2000 surge. The bear-market signposts that matter most now are credit spreads turning higher from complacent tights and a PMI rollover. The first is starting at the bottom of the quality ladder; the second has not happened.

⚔️Iran War

The war passed Day 220 on October 5 (GlobalSecurity). Parliament speaker Qalibaf says the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions from the June Memorandum of Understanding with the US are met. FM Araghchi has said it could reopen within seven days if they are, and Deputy FM Gharibabadi confirmed Tehran is evaluating a US response. President Pezeshkian has ruled out direct talks, and a third tanker in two days was hit near Hormuz (Iran International, Oct 3). Senior US officials led by VP Vance met at Camp David to discuss next steps (CBS). Two Iranian UN delegation members were expelled from the US. Washington has scaled back military operations in favor of economic pressure after heavy bombardment failed to end the war. In Yemen, the Houthis dispute Saudi-backed claims of retaken ground and claim strikes on a Saudi airport and refinery, yet CBS reports oil prices easing despite the fighting. Market read: the oil drop reflects a shift away from US kinetic escalation and the possibility of a conditional Hormuz reopening, not an actual reopening. That leaves headline risk skewed to oil upside.

Sources: Iran War 2026 -- Day 220 Update -- 05 October 2026 (GlobalSecurity) · Live - Pezeshkian rules out US talks as third tanker in two days hit near Hormuz (Iran International) · Senior Trump administration officials met to discuss Iran war at Camp David (CBS News) · Iran-backed Houthis deny losing ground in Yemen as oil prices ease despite fierce fighting (CBS News) · Early Edition: October 5, 2026 (Just Security) · 2026 Iran war (Wikipedia)

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Analyst estimate (inferred): a hold at the next FOMC meeting is slightly more likely than a second consecutive 25bp hike, roughly 55/45. The cooling core-trend measures and falling oil argue for patience. The 2Y at 4.7871, well above the 3.75–4.00% target range, implies the market still prices further tightening.

~1 YEAR

Analyst estimate (inferred): policy stays restrictive over the next 12 months, with one to two more hikes possible if core PCE (3.01%) doesn't converge, and no cuts until clear progress toward 2%. Consistent with his stated preference for a 'quieter' Fed, expect less forward guidance and continued balance-sheet restraint.

On the record: at the September 16, 2026 FOMC, the Committee raised the funds rate by 25bp to 3.75–4.00%, saying the move 'supports a timelier return' to 2% (Fed press conference transcript). Schwab reports the vote was 12-0. In his August 28 Jackson Hole keynote, Warsh said that despite good summer prints he saw strong underlying inflation trends and insufficient progress on PCE, and argued for a 'quieter' central bank (CNBC; Fed speech). In June he said 'inflation is too high' when the Fed raised rates for the first time in three years (PBS). Inferred: Warsh's reaction function weighs underlying trend over single prints. Today's falling core-trend gauges and the oil retreat give him room to pause, but he has shown he will move again if PCE stalls. I found no verified October 2026 Warsh remarks.
